text: Write a program that shows why `==` on strings sometimes works, which is worse than never working. Fill in the three blanks.
choices: System.out.println(___);            // compile-time constant: folded and interned
System.out.println(___);            // a fresh object: different identity
explanation: Verified: true, false, true. The first is true because the compiler folds the constant expression and interns the result, so both sides are literally the same object. That is why `==` on strings appears to work in small tests and fails on strings that arrive from input at run time — the worst possible behaviour, since testing does not catch it. Chapter 20 gives the general rule: `==` asks about identity, `equals` asks about value.
